title: N.S. senior killed ailing wife after promising to help her take her own life, court hears
summary: Douglas Smith, 75, was sentenced Tuesday for killing his wife in their home four years ago after she had asked for help taking her own life, according to court documents.

image.caption: Douglas Smith, 75, has been senteced to six years in prison for the death of his wife Iris Dodd in their home in Kingsport, N.S. on April 30, 2022. (Jeorge Sadi/CBC)

blocks.text: Nova Scotia·New
Douglas Smith, 75, was sentenced Tuesday for killing his wife in their home four years ago after she had asked for help taking her own life, according to court documents.
Douglas Smith, 75, sentenced Tuesday to 6 years for manslaughter
WARNING: This story includes references to suicide and details a killing.
A 75-year-old man smothered his ailing wife in their Kingsport, N.S., home more than four years ago after she made him promise to help her take her own life, a court was told Tuesday.

Douglas Smith was sentenced in Nova Scotia Supreme Court in Kentville, N.S., to six years in prison for the death of Iris Dodd, 72, on April 30, 2022. He pleaded guilty to manslaughter in April days before he was set to stand trial for second-degree murder.
Smith and Dodd, who had serious health issues, had been married for 33 years but faced eviction and had nowhere to go, according to an agreed statement of facts.
Court documents illustrate a harrowing situation the couple, who had a "long, supportive and happy life together," found themselves in that night.
Dodd’s health had been deteriorating since she suffered a stroke in 2018 and they were going to be kicked out of their home the next day, the documents say.
She used a wheelchair, was losing her eyesight and lived with chronic pain from arthritis and fibromyalgia — a long-term condition that causes muscle pain, extreme fatigue and sleep difficulty.
She had just had a long stay in hospital due to bouts of pneumonia.
On the night she died, court documents say Dodd told her husband she didn’t want to spend her final years in a health-care or long-term care facility.
She told Smith she planned to take all of her medication at once in an attempt to overdose and Smith should leave the house so he wouldn't be culpable.
The only thing she needed from her husband was for him to arrange the pills because she couldn’t see them very well.
Initially, the documents say, Smith didn’t support his wife’s plan when she raised the topic abruptly.
However, “The victim was very upset and made Mr. Smith promise to help her with her plan and he promised he would,” said the agreed statement of facts.
They couple agreed they’d go ahead with the plan the following day, which helped Dodd calm down and go to sleep.
Smith couldn’t sleep, though, worrying about his wife dying alone. He became increasingly concerned her plan might fail and leave her with permanent brain damage.
“Mr. Smith resolved all these thoughts and fears in his head by getting up and holding a pillow over the victim’s face,” the agreed statement of facts said.
‘She was in distress and I eased her distress’
The day after Smith killed Dodd, he drove to the local RCMP detachment to turn himself in.
After discovering the office was closed, he called 911 from the parking lot and admitted to taking her life.
A recording of Smith's 911 call was released by the court.
The call began with a dispatcher asking Smith what emergency he was reporting. The senior replied that he wanted to report a death.
The dispatcher asked if the death had been sudden or unexpected and Smith said that his wife had died and he was responsible.
Smith said he didn’t want to provide any details but the dispatcher said she required some information before an officer could be sent to meet him.
“She was in distress and I eased her distress,” Smith replied.
An officer came out of the detachment, arrested Smith and took him to a cell inside the building where Smith confirmed it was his voice on the 911 call, according to court documents.
Emotional day in court
Smith was emotional in court Tuesday, holding his head in his hands while the agreed statement of facts was read.
He wept when Crown prosecutor Daniel Rideout reached the part detailing how Smith had smothered his wife.
Smith was asked if he wanted a break but replied: "Let's get this over with."

blocks.text: During submissions, Rideout noted the case differed from the spate of domestic homicides in Nova Scotia in recent years.
Smith was driven by compassion when he took his wife's life, but he still broke the law and had other options available, Rideout said.
